newsitem.title: UK: UK stocks outlook - braced for interest rate rise.
newsitem.headline: UK stocks outlook - braced for interest rate rise.

text.p: Participants in the British equity market will be hoping for a steadier performance next week, after a run of extreme volatility sparked by the first budget under a Labour government for 18 years.

Yet with interest rates expected to be jacked up at next week's meeting of the Bank of England's monetary policy committee -- perhaps by as much as a half point -- the market could still be vulnerable to some sharp swings.

Despite some negative surprises in the budget, most notably Chancellor (finance minister) Gordon Brown's decision to abolish the tax credit for pension funds on dividends, the FTSE 100 index ended the week hitting record highs.

The market's resilience to the tax blow took many dealers and investors by surprise and shares may find it difficult to make progress from current levels against a backdrop of rising rates and continuing strength in sterling.
At U.S. investment bank JP Morgan, investment strategists Gary Dugan and Caroline Meroz this week cut their rating on UK shares to "underweight" from "neutral."
The JP Morgan analysts argued that the UK was the only market in Europe facing problems of a substantially appreciating currency, rising interest rates and falling corporate profit forecasts.
Yet there remains a deep divergence of view over the market's short-to-medium term prospects and some say there is no reason to be bearish yet.
Despite its gains, the FTSE 100 has underperformed other leading markets this year, leaving some to argue that the bad news has already been discounted.

"The strength of the pound is the market's biggest worry but we think it will weaken," said Richard Davidson, strategist at Morgan Stanley, who said he remained positive on the UK market's long-term prospects.
"Rates are going up but the relationship between short rates and equity performance is never that strong," he said, "and the valuation case is against continental European markets."
On Friday the FTSE 100 hit an intraday record of 4,879.0, up six percent on the week and up 18 percent since the end of 1996. During the week, it swung through a hefty 217-point range.

Richard Jeffrey, economist and strategist at Charterhouse Tilney, said he expected a rate rise from the newly-independent Bank of England next week as it battles to prevent the economy overheating -- just a month after the last increase.
"I think interest rates will be raised by half a point," said Jeffrey. "I think the Bank of England will try to give a strong signal and surprise people a bit."
The UK's base lending rate was last raised by a quarter point to 6.5 percent on June 6 in the wake of Labour's landslide election victory.
British economic reports in the coming week will be subject to particular study in the light of upward pressure on rates.

Monday's industrial production report for June was expected to show a rise of 0.8 percent on the month before, while Tuesday's retail prices report was forecast to show the annual headline inflation rate at 2.8 percent, up from 2.6 percent.
The underlying inflation rate, excluding mortgage interest payments, was forecast at 2.5 percent, unchanged from June.
In the U.S., it is a relatively quiet week for economic reports and the main release is producer prices for June on Friday, seen unchanged on the month.
FTSE 100 companies reporting next week include industrial conglomerate Tomkins, electrical retailer Dixons Group Plc, and defence-to-electronics group General Electric Co Plc.
